title: Content Security Policy and Subresource Integrity
objectives: Write a strict Content Security Policy with nonces or hashes instead of host allowlists
Roll a policy out safely with report-only mode and violation reports
Pin third-party files with Subresource Integrity and know when it breaks

cards.title: A second wall behind output encoding
cards.body: Escaping output stops most cross-site scripting, but one missed spot is enough for an attacker’s script to run with the page’s full privileges. A Content Security Policy is a response header that tells the browser which scripts may run. If injected markup slips through, the browser refuses to execute it, so a single bug no longer becomes account takeover.

cards.title: Misconception: an allowlist of trusted hosts is enough
cards.body: A policy like script-src self cdn.example.com feels strict, but any allowed host that serves user-controlled files, old library versions or callback endpoints lets an attacker load script from there. Google researchers who studied deployed policies found that most host-allowlist policies could be bypassed. A strict policy instead says: only scripts carrying this response’s random nonce, or matching a known hash, may run.

cards.title: How a nonce-based policy decides
cards.body: Each response gets a fresh secret; only scripts that carry it run.
steps: Server generates 16 random bytes for this response only
Header: script-src with that nonce, plus strict-dynamic; object-src none; base-uri none
Every script tag the server writes carries the same nonce attribute
Injected script tags lack the nonce, so the browser blocks them
Scripts loaded by a trusted script are allowed through strict-dynamic

cards.title: Worked example: hashes for a cached page
cards.body: A marketing page is static HTML cached on a CDN for an hour. A nonce would be reused for every visitor during that hour, so anyone who read the page would know it. Instead, the build computes a SHA-256 hash of each inline script and lists the hashes in the policy. Changing one byte of a script changes its hash, so the build must regenerate the header whenever scripts change.

cards.title: Subresource Integrity: pin the exact bytes
cards.body: A script or stylesheet tag can carry an integrity attribute with a hash such as sha384 followed by a base64 digest. The browser downloads the file, hashes it and refuses to use it if the hash differs. Cross-origin files must be requested in CORS mode, so the tag also needs the crossorigin attribute and the host must send the matching CORS header.

cards.title: Trap: enforcing on day one
cards.body: Switching a policy straight to enforcing breaks whatever you forgot: an analytics snippet, an inline handler attribute, a payment widget. Ship it first as Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only, collect violation reports for a week or two, fix or allow what is legitimate, then enforce. Expect noise from browser extensions in the reports and filter it out.

questions.prompt: A team’s policy allows scripts from its own origin and a large public CDN. Why might it still fail to stop an injected script?

choices.label: Browsers ignore Content Security Policy headers on pages served over HTTPS
The CDN hosts old libraries and callback endpoints an attacker can load instead
An allowlist only restricts stylesheets and fonts, while scripts need a separate header
The header must be repeated on each image and font response

questions.explanation: Allowlisted hosts often serve script an attacker can reuse; a nonce or hash ties execution to scripts the server wrote. HTTPS does not disable the policy, script-src covers scripts, and the policy belongs on the document response.

questions.prompt: What makes a nonce-based policy secure?

choices.label: The nonce is long and the same for all users, so it is hard to guess
The nonce is stored in a session cookie, and the server checks it on each script request
A fresh unpredictable value per response, so an attacker cannot know it in advance
The nonce is encrypted with the site’s TLS certificate

questions.explanation: Security comes from unpredictability per response. A shared nonce can be read from any copy of the page; the browser, not the server, checks the attribute; TLS keys are unrelated.

questions.prompt: A static page is cached on a CDN for an hour and has two small inline scripts. Which policy fits best?

choices.label: Allow the two scripts by listing their SHA-256 hashes
Use a nonce, since the CDN reuses it for an hour
Add unsafe-inline so both scripts keep working
Skip the policy because the page is static

questions.explanation: Hashes describe the script content, so they survive caching. A cached nonce is shared by all visitors, unsafe-inline allows injected scripts too, and static pages can still render untrusted data such as query strings.

questions.prompt: A tag loads a library from another origin with an integrity hash, but the browser refuses it after the vendor fixes a typo in the file. What happened?

choices.label: The vendor’s TLS certificate expired during the fix
The policy header blocked the vendor’s origin
The file was cached under the old hash by the CDN
The changed bytes no longer match the pinned hash

questions.explanation: Integrity checks the exact bytes. That is the point, and why it suits versioned files whose content never changes; an unversioned URL that the vendor edits will break.

questions.prompt: Order a safe rollout of a strict policy.

items.label: Review violation reports and fix legitimate breakages
Add nonces or hashes to the scripts you serve
Switch the header to enforcing and keep reporting on
Send the policy in report-only mode

questions.explanation: Make your own scripts compliant, observe without breaking anything, fix what reports reveal, then enforce while still watching reports.

questions.prompt: An integrity value uses SHA-384, a 48-byte digest, written in base64. How many base64 characters is the digest?
assumptions: Base64 writes every 3 bytes as 4 characters
48 is divisible by 3, so there is no padding
questions.explanation: Sanity check: base64 is about a third longer than the raw bytes, so 48 bytes becomes 64 characters.

flashcards.back: script-src with a per-response nonce or script hashes, plus strict-dynamic; object-src none; base-uri none.
Nonce for HTML rendered per request; hash for static or cached HTML.
Report-only first, read violation reports, fix, then enforce.
A hash on a script or stylesheet tag; the browser rejects the file if its bytes differ.

sources.title: web.dev: Mitigate cross-site scripting with a strict Content Security Policy
ACM CCS 2016: CSP Is Dead, Long Live CSP!

mechanism.title: How the browser enforces a policy
steps: The server sends a Content-Security-Policy header with the document. Each directive covers one kind of resource: script-src for scripts, style-src for styles, connect-src for network requests made by script, frame-ancestors for who may embed the page, and so on. When the page tries to run or load something, the browser checks the matching directive and blocks anything not allowed, reporting the violation if a reporting endpoint is set.

A strict policy bases script trust on the response rather than on hosts. With a nonce, the server generates at least 128 bits of randomness per response, puts it in the header, and writes it as an attribute on every script tag it emits. Injected markup cannot know the value, so it does not run. Inline event handler attributes and script URLs are blocked as well, so those must move into script files or nonced blocks.

With strict-dynamic, a script trusted by nonce or hash may load further scripts, and those are trusted too; host allowlists are then ignored by browsers that support it. This keeps loaders and tag managers working without listing every host. Adding unsafe-inline and https: as fallbacks is a common pattern: browsers that understand nonces ignore them, while very old browsers fall back to them.

Hashes are the alternative for pages that cannot carry a fresh nonce, such as HTML cached on a CDN. The policy lists a SHA-256, SHA-384 or SHA-512 digest of each inline script, and the browser hashes each script it sees and runs it only on a match. Builds must regenerate the hashes whenever a script changes, or the change will be blocked.

Subresource Integrity applies the same idea to files: a script or stylesheet tag carries the expected hash, and the browser refuses the file if the downloaded bytes differ. Cross-origin files must be fetched in CORS mode for the check to run. Report-only mode sends the same policy under a different header name, which reports violations without blocking, so a team can see what would break before enforcing.

useWhen: Any site that renders user content or has a large front-end codebase.
Pages loading versioned third-party files that must not change silently.
avoidWhen: Avoid nonces on HTML that a shared cache serves to many users; use hashes.
Avoid integrity hashes on unversioned vendor URLs that change in place.

rows: Long lists that drift as vendors change
Per-response nonce in header and tags
Breaks on any change to the pinned file

numbers.title: Sizing a nonce and an integrity value
assumptions: Nonce of 16 random bytes, the 128-bit minimum the specification recommends
Integrity digest from SHA-384, which is 48 bytes
Base64 writes 3 bytes as 4 characters, padding the final group
steps: Nonce: 16 bytes is 5 full groups of 3 plus 1 byte, so 6 groups × 4 = 24 characters including padding.
Guessing it: 2 to the power 128 possibilities, far beyond any attacker.
Integrity: 48 ÷ 3 = 16 groups, 16 × 4 = 64 characters with no padding.
Header cost: a strict policy is around 150 bytes, small next to a typical document.
numbers.result: Strong protection costs a few dozen characters per response; the real cost is the work to remove inline handlers and keep hashes current.

india.title: Research on deployed policies
india.label: Public research (ACM CCS 2016)
india.body: In the paper “CSP Is Dead, Long Live CSP!”, presented at the ACM Conference on Computer and Communications Security in 2016, Google researchers analysed policies collected from a very large crawl of the web and reported that the large majority of policies relying on host allowlists could be bypassed, largely because allowed hosts served script an attacker could reuse. The paper proposed nonce-based policies with strict-dynamic, which web.dev now documents as a strict policy.

pitfalls.trap: “We list our CDN in script-src, so we are safe.”
pitfalls.say: “Anything that CDN serves can run; I’d trust scripts by nonce or hash instead.”

pitfalls.trap: “Let’s enforce the new policy on Monday.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d run it in report-only mode first and fix what the reports show.”

pitfalls.trap: “Add an integrity hash to the vendor’s latest-version URL.”
pitfalls.say: “Only pin versioned files; an edited file will be blocked.”

takeaways: A policy is the second wall behind output encoding.
Trust scripts by per-response nonce or by hash, not by host.
Use hashes when HTML is cached and shared.
Roll out in report-only mode, then enforce.
Integrity hashes pin exact bytes, so use them on versioned files.

interactive.title: Which script runs?
interactive.prompt: A page is served with script-src using a nonce and strict-dynamic. A comment field has an escaping bug, and an attacker’s comment contains a script tag with no nonce. The page’s own loader script, which carries the nonce, then creates a script element for a chat widget from another host and appends it to the page.

choices.label: The chat widget runs; the injected script is blocked
choices.feedback: Right: strict-dynamic passes trust from the nonced loader to what it loads, while markup without the nonce is blocked.

choices.label: Both run, because the page has an escaping bug
choices.feedback: The policy is checked by the browser regardless of how the markup got there.

choices.label: Neither runs, because the chat host is not listed
choices.feedback: With strict-dynamic, supporting browsers ignore host lists and trust scripts added by trusted scripts.

interactive.reveal: The nonce identifies scripts the server wrote. Injected markup cannot guess it, and strict-dynamic lets trusted code load what it needs without a host allowlist.

seeAlso.why: The XSS attacks a policy is designed to contain
Third-party scripts that a policy and integrity hashes help contain
CORS, which integrity checks on cross-origin files depend on

title: Web Fonts Without Invisible Text or Layout Shift
objectives: Explain why web fonts are discovered late and how the block and swap periods behave
Choose a font-display value for body text, headings and icon fonts
Cut font bytes with WOFF2, subsetting and fewer weights, and match fallback metrics to stop shifts

cards.title: Why text can be invisible
cards.body: A browser only requests a web font once it has the HTML, has parsed the CSS, and has found text that uses that font. Until the file arrives, the font is in its block period: most browsers draw the text invisibly for up to about 3 seconds before falling back to a system font. On a slow connection the page has layout and images but no words.

cards.title: The font timeline for one face
cards.body: font-display chooses how long each period lasts.
steps: Block period: text is drawn invisibly while the font loads
Swap period: the fallback font is shown; the web font replaces it if it arrives
Failure period: the fallback stays for the rest of the page view
swap: almost no block, unlimited swap
optional: about 100 ms block, no swap, so a late font is skipped for this view

cards.title: Worked example: four weights on a slow phone
cards.body: A page uses regular, italic, semibold and bold, each a 40 KB WOFF2 file: 160 KB. At 1.6 Mbit/s that is 160 × 8 ÷ 1,600 = 0.8 s of transfer, after three round trips of discovery (HTML, CSS, font) at 150 ms each, 0.45 s. Dropping to two weights and a Latin-only subset of 25 KB each brings transfer to 50 × 8 ÷ 1,600 = 0.25 s, and a preload removes one discovery round trip.

cards.title: Matching the fallback so the swap does not shift
cards.body: When the web font swaps in, lines rewrap if the two fonts have different widths and heights, and everything below moves: a layout shift. @font-face descriptors such as size-adjust, ascent-override, descent-override and line-gap-override let you declare a local fallback scaled to the web font’s metrics, so the swap changes the look of the letters but barely moves the lines.

cards.title: Trap: preloading without crossorigin
cards.body: Fonts are always fetched in CORS mode, even from your own origin. A preload hint without the crossorigin attribute is a different request, so the browser downloads the font once for the preload, cannot use it, and downloads it again for the CSS. Preload only the one or two faces used above the fold, with crossorigin and the right type.

cards.title: Edge case: icon fonts and swap
cards.body: For an icon font, swapping to a fallback shows random letters where icons belong, and the user may read “search” as a stray character. Use block for icon fonts, or better, replace them with inline SVG icons, which need no font download and carry their own accessible names.

questions.prompt: Body text must be readable as soon as possible, and a later swap to the brand font is acceptable. Which font-display value fits?

choices.label: block
swap
auto
optional

questions.explanation: swap shows the fallback almost at once and swaps the web font in when it arrives. block hides text for up to about 3 s, auto usually behaves like block, and optional may skip the brand font for this view.

questions.prompt: Why is a font referenced from a stylesheet requested later than an image in the HTML?

choices.label: Fonts are low priority until all images have loaded
Font files are larger than images, so the browser defers them until images finish
The browser must parse the CSS and find text using the font before requesting it
Fonts can only load after the page’s scripts have run

questions.explanation: The font URL sits inside CSS and is fetched only when matching text is styled; preload lets the HTML announce it early. Fonts are not deferred for being large and do not wait for scripts.

questions.prompt: After a web font swaps in, a paragraph rewraps from 6 lines to 7 and pushes a button down. What fixes the shift while keeping the brand font?

choices.label: Switch font-display from swap to block for that face so no swap is seen
Add a preconnect hint for the font host
Convert the font file from WOFF2 to TrueType
Scale a local fallback with size-adjust and metric overrides

questions.explanation: Matching the fallback’s metrics keeps line breaks close, so the swap barely moves anything. With block, lines are still laid out with the invisible fallback and reflow when the font arrives, so it hides text for longer without fixing the shift; preconnect only speeds the download, and TrueType files are larger.

questions.prompt: Which change cuts font bytes the most for an English-only site using six weights of a family?

choices.label: Two weights in WOFF2, subset to the Latin range
Gzip the WOFF2 files on the server
Add a long cache lifetime to the font files
Load the fonts from a public font CDN

questions.explanation: Fewer files, a compact format and only the needed characters cut bytes directly. WOFF2 is already compressed, caching helps only repeat visits, and browsers partition caches by site, so a public CDN copy is not shared with other sites.

questions.prompt: Order the steps before a web font can paint text on a first visit.

items.label: Download the font file
Download and parse the stylesheet
Swap from the fallback or end the block period
Download and parse the HTML
Match text to a rule using the font face

questions.explanation: HTML, then CSS, then matching text, then the font request, then rendering with it: three sequential steps a preload can shorten.

questions.prompt: Four font files of 40 KB each download at 1.6 Mbit/s. About how many milliseconds does the transfer take, ignoring round trips?
assumptions: 1 KB = 1,000 bytes for this estimate
The link is the only bottleneck
questions.workedAnswer: 160 KB × 8 = 1,280 kbit; 1,280 kbit ÷ 1,600 kbit/s = 0.8 s, which is 800 ms
questions.explanation: Sanity check: a fifth of a megabyte on a slow mobile link is close to a second, before any discovery round trips.

flashcards.back: HTML, then CSS, then matching text, then the font request.
swap shows the fallback and swaps later; optional skips a font that misses about 100 ms.
Add crossorigin and the type; fonts are fetched in CORS mode.
Scale a local fallback with size-adjust and ascent, descent and line-gap overrides.

mechanism.title: How a font goes from CSS to pixels
steps: An @font-face rule only declares that a face exists. The browser downloads it lazily: after the HTML and the stylesheet are parsed, during style calculation it finds an element whose text uses that family, weight and style, and only then requests the file. Faces declared but unused cost nothing, while the ones used cost three steps of discovery before any bytes flow.

While a face loads, font-display decides what the user sees. The specification defines a block period, when text is laid out with an invisible fallback; a swap period, when the fallback is visible and the web font replaces it if it arrives; and a failure period, when the fallback stays. block uses a short block period, about 3 s, then swaps; swap has a block period close to zero; fallback blocks for about 100 ms and swaps for about 3 s; optional blocks for about 100 ms and does not swap, so a slow font is used only on a later visit once it is cached.

Bytes are the next lever. WOFF2 uses a stronger compression than WOFF or raw TrueType, so it is the format to serve. Subsetting removes glyphs the site does not use, and unicode-range in each @font-face lets the browser fetch a subset only when the page contains characters in its range. Each weight and style is a separate file unless you use a variable font, which carries many weights in one file and often pays off once a page uses several weights; compare the bytes, since one variable file can outweigh two static ones.

Discovery can be shortened. A preload hint in the HTML starts the font request in the first round trip, but it needs the crossorigin attribute because fonts use CORS mode, and preloading more than one or two faces steals bandwidth from the stylesheet and hero image. Self-hosting on your own origin avoids a new connection to a font host; browsers now partition the HTTP cache by site, so a font on a shared CDN is not reused across sites.

The swap itself can shift layout. A fallback such as a system sans-serif usually has different character widths and line heights from the web font, so text rewraps when it swaps. Declaring a local fallback face with size-adjust, ascent-override, descent-override and line-gap-override, using values computed from the web font’s metrics, makes the two occupy nearly the same space.

useWhen: Brand typography on content pages where text must appear fast.
Pages with Core Web Vitals problems from late text or layout shifts.
avoidWhen: Avoid swap for icon fonts; use block or replace them with SVG.
Avoid preloading every face; preload only what renders above the fold.

rows: Invisible text for up to about 3 s
Short block, swap within about 3 s
Fallback unless the font is almost instant
Brand font may be missing on first visit

numbers.title: What a font family costs on a slow phone
assumptions: 1.6 Mbit/s link, 150 ms round trip (illustrative slow mobile profile)
Four WOFF2 faces of 40 KB each before optimisation
Two faces of 25 KB each after subsetting to Latin
steps: Discovery: HTML, CSS and font requests in sequence, 3 × 150 ms = 450 ms.
Transfer before: 160 KB × 8 ÷ 1,600 kbit/s = 800 ms.
Transfer after: 50 KB × 8 ÷ 1,600 kbit/s = 250 ms.
With a preload the font request starts with the CSS, saving about one round trip of 150 ms.
numbers.result: From about 1.25 s to about 0.55 s before the brand font can paint: fewer faces, smaller files and earlier discovery.

india.title: Guidance from the browser teams
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: web.dev’s best practices for fonts recommend serving WOFF2, self-hosting, subsetting with unicode-range, preloading only critical faces and choosing font-display to match how important the font is. MDN documents the block, swap and failure periods, and the CSS Fonts Module Level 4 defines the size-adjust and metric override descriptors used to make a fallback face match a web font so the swap does not cause layout shift.

pitfalls.trap: “Use font-display: swap everywhere.”
pitfalls.say: “Swap for text; icon fonts need block or should become SVG.”

pitfalls.trap: “Preload all six faces so they are ready.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d preload the one used above the fold, with crossorigin, and cut the rest.”

pitfalls.trap: “A shared font CDN is probably already cached.”
pitfalls.say: “Caches are partitioned by site now; I’d self-host.”

takeaways: Fonts are found only after HTML, CSS and matching text.
font-display sets the block and swap periods; swap suits body text.
Serve WOFF2, subset, and use as few faces as possible.
Preload one or two critical faces with crossorigin.
Match fallback metrics so the swap does not shift layout.

interactive.title: How much do fonts cost?
interactive.prompt: A slow phone needs three round trips of 150 ms to discover a web font (HTML, CSS, font) and then downloads at 1.6 Mbit/s. Slide the total size of the font files the page uses.
interactive.takeaway: At 160 KB the bytes take 800 ms after 450 ms of discovery; at 50 KB they take 250 ms, so cutting faces and subsetting matters more than any hint, and a preload then trims the discovery.

seeAlso.why: Preload and preconnect hints in the wider loading picture
How a font swap shows up as layout shift
Scripts and character ranges that subsets must cover

title: Client-Side Routing: History, Deep Links, Scroll and Focus
objectives: Explain how a single-page app changes the URL without a full page load
Make deep links, refresh and the back button work, including the server fallback and real 404s
Restore scroll position and move focus on route changes so the app behaves like real pages

cards.title: The page you replaced did a lot for free
cards.body: A full page load resets scroll to the top, restores it on back, moves focus to the new document, announces the new title to screen readers, and lets the server answer any URL. A client-side router intercepts link clicks, pushes a new history entry and renders the next view in place. It is faster, but every one of those free behaviours now has to be rebuilt by hand.

cards.title: One client-side navigation
cards.body: What a router must do for each link click.
steps: Intercept a plain click on a real link; let modified clicks open a new tab
Save the current scroll position against the current history entry
Push the new URL as a history entry and fetch the view’s data
Render the view, set the document title and move focus to its main heading
On back or forward, render the entry’s view and restore its saved scroll

cards.title: Worked example: the refresh that returns 404
cards.body: A user is on /orders/42 and presses refresh. The browser now asks the server for /orders/42, a path the router invented. A static host with only index.html at the root replies 404. The fix is a rewrite: any path that is not a file returns the app shell, so the router can render the order. Unknown paths should still end with a real 404 status, served by the server or rendered with a noindex page, or search engines index error pages as if they were content.

cards.title: Push or replace?
cards.body: Push a new entry when the user would expect back to return here: opening a product, changing a tab of content. Replace the current entry for refinements, such as each keystroke in a filter or a redirect after login. Pushing on every keystroke of a 12-letter search leaves 12 entries, and the back button seems broken.

cards.title: Trap: buttons pretending to be links
cards.body: A clickable element that is not a link with an href cannot be opened in a new tab, copied, bookmarked or followed by a crawler, and screen readers do not announce it as a link. Render real links and intercept only plain primary-button clicks with no modifier keys; let Ctrl, Cmd, Shift and middle clicks reach the browser.

cards.title: Edge case: slow data and fast clicks
cards.body: The user clicks Orders, then Settings before the orders data arrives. If the orders response then renders, the URL says Settings and the screen shows orders. Give each navigation an id and render only the latest one, cancelling or ignoring older data requests, exactly as for search-as-you-type.

questions.prompt: Refreshing /settings/profile on a single-page app returns 404, while the home page works. What is the usual fix?

choices.label: Add a cache lifetime so the browser keeps the page
Have the server return the app shell for paths that are not files
Move all routes into the fragment after the hash sign for search engines
Register the route in the browser’s history before refreshing

questions.explanation: The server must answer any app path with the shell (or a server-rendered page). Caching does not create a missing route, and history entries live only in the browser. Hash routes would avoid the 404, because the server never sees the fragment, but search engines do not index fragment routes as separate pages, so moving to them “for search engines” gets it backwards.

questions.prompt: A product list updates its URL as the user ticks filters. Which history behaviour fits?

choices.label: Push one entry per filter click so back undoes each click
Keep the URL unchanged so history stays clean
Replace the current entry, so back leaves the filtered list
Open a new tab for each filter combination

questions.explanation: Filters refine one view, so replace keeps the URL shareable without filling history. Pushing makes back step through every tick, and not updating the URL loses shareable filtered links.

questions.prompt: After a client-side route change, a screen reader user hears nothing and keeps tabbing through the old menu. What should the router add?

choices.label: A louder notification sound on each navigation
A higher z-index for the new view
A full page reload on navigation for screen reader users only
Update the title and move focus to the new view’s heading

questions.explanation: A full load would move focus and announce the new title; a router must do both itself. Sound and stacking order do not move focus, and detecting assistive technology is unreliable.

questions.prompt: A user scrolls far down a feed, opens a post, then presses back and lands at the top. What went wrong?

choices.label: The router did not save and restore scroll for that history entry
The feed’s images were not lazy-loaded
The back button reloaded the feed from the server, losing its position
The post page used a different stylesheet

questions.explanation: With client-side routing the app owns scroll restoration: save the position per entry and restore it after the feed re-renders, which may require its data to be cached. Lazy-loading images affects bytes, not the saved position; back in a single-page app re-renders from history rather than reloading the page; and a stylesheet does not store scroll.

questions.prompt: Order what a router does when a user clicks an in-app link.

items.label: Push the new URL onto history
Move focus to the new view’s main heading
Check it is a plain click on a same-origin link
Render the new view and update the title
Save the scroll position of the current entry

questions.explanation: Decide to handle the click, remember where the user was, change the URL, render, then restore what a page load would have done for focus and title.

questions.prompt: A search box pushes a new history entry on every keystroke. A user types a 12-letter word and then wants to go back to the previous page. How many presses of back does that take?
assumptions: The search started on a page with no query in the URL
Each keystroke pushes one entry
questions.formula: 12 entries for keystrokes + 1 to leave the page
questions.workedAnswer: 12 presses walk back through the keystrokes to the empty search; 1 more leaves: 13
questions.explanation: Sanity check: with replace it takes 1 press, which is what users expect.

flashcards.back: Rewrite app paths to the shell, but return a real 404 for unknown ones.
Push for places users go back to; replace for filters, typing and redirects.
Set the title, move focus to the main heading, restore or reset scroll.

sources.title: WHATWG HTML: Session history and navigation

mechanism.title: What a router replaces
steps: The browser keeps a session history: a list of entries, each with a URL and optional state. A client-side router adds entries with the history push operation and swaps the current one with replace; neither makes a request. When the user presses back or forward, the browser moves along the list and fires a pop-state event, and the router renders the view for that entry’s URL.

Links stay real links with href attributes, so the browser’s own features keep working: open in new tab, copy address, hover preview, crawlers. The router intercepts only primary-button clicks without modifier keys on same-origin links, and lets downloads, external links and new-tab clicks through. This keeps progressive behaviour if the script fails to load.

Every URL the router can produce must also work as a first request. The server either renders the page for that path or returns the application shell, which reads the URL and renders the right view. Paths that match no route should still produce a 404 status, or a page marked not to be indexed, because returning 200 with an error message creates soft 404s that search engines treat as real pages.

Scroll and focus were the browser’s job and become the router’s. Browsers offer automatic scroll restoration, but it runs before an asynchronously rendered view exists, so many apps set it to manual, save the position per entry, scroll to the top for new navigations, honour fragment links, and restore saved positions after the old view renders again.

A full navigation moves focus to the new document and screen readers announce its title. A router should set the document title and move focus to the main heading of the new view (made focusable for that purpose) or announce the change through a polite live region. Navigations can overlap, so each gets an id and only the latest one may render.

useWhen: Apps with long-lived state such as editors, dashboards and mail, where full reloads lose context.
Sites where navigations should feel instant after the first load.
avoidWhen: Avoid for mostly static content sites where full page loads are already fast.
Avoid fragment-only routing for public pages that need indexing and clean links.

rows: Server must return the shell or render the path
App saves and restores per entry
App sets title and moves focus
Only data and code for the new view

numbers.title: History entries from a search box
assumptions: The search page is reached from a home page
The user types 12 letters
Each pushed entry costs one press of back
steps: Pushing per keystroke adds 12 entries on top of the empty search page.
Leaving the search: 12 presses to reach the empty search plus 1 to reach home = 13.
Replacing per keystroke and pushing once when the search is submitted: 1 press to leave.
Debouncing so the URL updates after 300 ms of no typing (an illustrative delay) keeps the shareable URL without the pile-up.
numbers.result: Push for places, replace for refinements: 13 presses of back become 1.

india.title: How the platform defines it
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: MDN’s History API documentation and the WHATWG HTML standard define session history entries, the push and replace operations, the pop-state event fired on back and forward, and the scroll restoration setting that lets an application take over restoring scroll positions. web.dev’s accessibility course describes moving focus to new content after in-page navigation so keyboard and screen reader users are not left on stale elements.

pitfalls.trap: “Back works, the router handles it.”
pitfalls.say: “Back renders the view, but I’d also restore scroll and move focus.”

pitfalls.trap: “Return index.html with 200 for every path.”
pitfalls.say: “Shell for real routes, a 404 status for unknown ones.”

pitfalls.trap: “Use a clickable div for navigation items.”
pitfalls.say: “Real links with href, intercepted only on plain clicks.”

takeaways: A router must rebuild scroll, focus, title and deep links itself.
Every app URL must work as a first request, and unknown ones return 404.
Push for places users return to; replace for refinements.
Keep real links and intercept only plain clicks.
Let only the latest navigation render.

interactive.title: What does refresh do?
interactive.prompt: A single-page app is deployed to a static file host that serves files only, with index.html at the root. A user opens the home page, clicks through to /orders/42 inside the app, then presses refresh.

choices.label: The order page reloads normally
choices.feedback: The browser now asks the server for /orders/42, and the host has no such file.

choices.label: The host returns 404 for /orders/42
choices.feedback: Right: the path only ever existed inside the router; the server needs a rewrite to the shell.

choices.label: The browser shows the cached home page
choices.feedback: Refresh requests the current URL, not the page the app started from.

interactive.reveal: Configure the host to return the app shell for app paths, or render them on the server, and keep a real 404 for paths no route matches.

seeAlso.why: How the shell and hydration relate to server rendering
Moving focus correctly when content changes
Ignoring stale responses when requests overlap

title: Internationalisation: Plurals, Dates, Numbers and Right-to-Left
objectives: Write translatable messages with named variables and plural categories instead of concatenation
Format numbers, currencies and dates by locale, and store instants and local times correctly
Build layouts that survive text expansion and right-to-left scripts

cards.title: Strings are not the whole job
cards.body: Translating a site is more than swapping words. Word order changes between languages, plural rules differ, numbers group digits differently, dates have different orders and calendars, and Arabic, Hebrew, Persian and Urdu run right to left. Code that glues strings together or formats numbers by hand breaks in ways a translator cannot fix.

cards.title: Misconception: plural means “one or many”
cards.body: English has two plural categories for counts, one and other. Unicode’s CLDR data defines up to six: zero, one, two, few, many and other. Arabic uses all six, Polish and Russian use one, few, many and other, Japanese uses only other, and French puts 0 in the same category as 1. A message such as “{count} files” needs one variant per category the language uses, chosen by the locale’s rules.

cards.title: Worked example: one number, four locales
cards.body: The number 1234567.891 is written 1,234,567.891 in US English, 1.234.567,891 in German, 1 234 567,891 in French (with narrow spaces) and 12,34,567.891 in Indian English, which groups by lakh and crore. Currency adds symbol position and decimals: Japanese yen has no minor unit. Use the platform’s locale-aware formatter with a locale and currency code, never string tricks.

cards.title: Times: instants versus local times
cards.body: A payment happened at an instant: store it in UTC and format it in the viewer’s time zone. A dentist appointment at 09:30 next March in Mumbai is a local time: store 09:30, the date and the IANA zone Asia/Kolkata, because offsets and daylight saving rules can change before then. A birthday is a date with no time; storing it as midnight UTC shows the previous day to users west of UTC.

cards.title: Building a layout that survives translation
cards.body: Design for growth and direction from the start.
steps: Set lang and dir on the root element from the chosen locale
Use logical properties: inline-start and inline-end instead of left and right
Let text wrap; avoid fixed widths for buttons and tabs
Mirror directional icons such as back arrows in right-to-left layouts
Isolate user-supplied text so a Hebrew name does not reorder an English sentence

cards.title: Trap: building sentences from pieces
cards.body: Code like “You have ” + n + “ new ” + noun gives translators fragments with no context, fixes English word order, and cannot handle plural or gender agreement. Use one message per sentence with named variables and plural or select cases, so the translator controls the whole sentence.

questions.prompt: A message shows “{count} files”. How many plural variants does an Arabic translation need?

choices.label: Two, like English
Three: zero, one and many
Six, one for each CLDR category
One, since the number is shown anyway

questions.explanation: Arabic uses zero, one, two, few, many and other. English needs two; a single variant would be wrong for most counts.

questions.prompt: A clinic app stores next year’s 09:30 appointment in Mumbai. What should it store?

choices.label: The UTC instant computed today from the current offset
The local date and time plus the zone id Asia/Kolkata
The local time as text in the viewer’s language
Only the date, with the time in a separate free-text note

questions.explanation: Future local events keep their wall-clock time and zone, so a change to the zone’s rules does not move them. A UTC instant fixed today can drift; text and notes cannot be computed with.

questions.prompt: Which output shows 1234567.5 correctly for Indian English?
questions.explanation: Indian English groups the last three digits, then pairs: lakh and crore. The others are US English, German and French grouping.

questions.prompt: A design system uses margin-left for the gap after an icon. What breaks in Arabic, and what is the fix?

choices.label: The gap lands on the wrong side; use margin-inline-end
The icon disappears; use a larger icon size
The text becomes unreadable; switch to a fixed-width font
Nothing breaks; browsers mirror margins in right-to-left text

questions.explanation: Physical properties stay physical; logical properties such as margin-inline-end follow the writing direction. Browsers do not swap left and right margins for you.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to render a translated “{count} new messages” string.

items.label: Choose the plural variant for count using the locale’s rules
Pick the user’s locale from settings or the language request header
Format count with the locale’s number formatter and insert it into the message
Load that locale’s message catalogue

questions.explanation: Locale first, then its messages, then the plural case for the number, then the formatted number in the sentence.

questions.prompt: A tab label is 10 characters in English. A common guideline from IBM, reproduced by the W3C, says strings this short can become two to three times longer in European languages. What width in characters should the tab allow at the upper end?
assumptions: Upper end of the guideline: 300% of the source length
Characters are roughly equal width in the font
questions.explanation: Sanity check: short labels grow the most; long paragraphs grow about 30%, so the tab needs far more slack than body text.

flashcards.back: zero, one, two, few, many, other; English uses one and other, Arabic all six.
An instant in UTC, formatted in the viewer’s zone.
Local date and time plus the IANA zone id.
dir on the root, logical properties, mirrored direction icons, isolated user text.

sources.title: W3C Internationalization: Structural markup and right-to-left text in HTML
W3C Internationalization: Text size in translation
MDN: CSS logical properties and values

mechanism.title: How a locale shapes what the user sees
steps: A locale identifier such as hi-IN, ar-EG or pt-BR names a language and optionally a region. The app chooses one from an explicit user setting first, then the browser’s language preference sent in the Accept-Language header; guessing from IP location alone annoys travellers and multilingual users. The choice selects a message catalogue and the formatting rules.

Messages are whole sentences with named variables such as {count}. Formats such as ICU MessageFormat add plural and select cases inside the message, so a translator writes each plural category or gendered form the language needs. The runtime picks the plural category from CLDR rules for the locale and number: 1 is one in English, 0 is one in French, 2 is two in Arabic, 5 is many in Russian.

Numbers, currencies, dates, lists and relative times are formatted by locale-aware formatters, which encode digit grouping, decimal separators, currency placement, month names, the order of day, month and year, and the default calendar and numbering system. Sorting needs locale collation too: Swedish sorts ä after z, while German sorts it with a.

Time needs a model before formatting. Instants such as a payment or a log entry are stored in UTC and shown in the viewer’s zone. Future wall-clock events are stored as local date and time plus an IANA zone id, so a rule change still yields 09:30 in that city. Date-only values such as birthdays are stored as dates, not midnights.

Layout must allow for both direction and length. Setting dir to rtl flips inline flow, and CSS logical properties such as margin-inline-start and inset-inline-end follow it, where left and right do not. Directional icons mirror; logos, clocks and media controls usually do not. Text in another direction inside a sentence is isolated so it does not reorder neighbours, and containers let translated text wrap rather than truncate.

useWhen: Products with users in more than one language, region or time zone.
Any product handling money, dates or counts shown to people.
avoidWhen: Avoid concatenating translated fragments into sentences.
Avoid fixed-width labels sized for English text.

rows: Locale formatter with a currency code
Local time plus IANA zone id

numbers.title: How much space translation needs
assumptions: Guideline from IBM’s global design guidance, as reproduced by the W3C (an estimate, not a rule)
Source strings of up to 10 characters grow to 200–300%
Source strings over 70 characters grow to about 130%
steps: A 10-character tab label may need up to 10 × 3 = 30 characters.
An 80-character sentence may need about 80 × 1.3 = 104 characters.
A row of five tabs at 30 characters each needs about three times the English width, so it must wrap or scroll.
Arabic counts need six plural variants per message, against two in English.
numbers.result: Short labels need the most slack: plan for roughly triple, and let containers wrap.

india.title: What the W3C reports about text length
india.label: Public guidance (W3C Internationalization)
india.body: The W3C Internationalization article on text size in translation reproduces IBM’s average expansion rates for text translated from English into European languages, from 200–300% for strings of up to 10 characters to about 130% for text over 70 characters, and gives an example where the Flickr label for “views” became 3 times longer in Italian. The W3C’s guidance on right-to-left text recommends setting dir on the html element and using markup that isolates text of unknown direction.

pitfalls.trap: “Plural is count == 1.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d use the locale’s plural categories; Arabic needs six forms.”

pitfalls.trap: “Store every time in UTC.”
pitfalls.say: “Instants yes; future local events keep their local time and zone.”

pitfalls.trap: “Our buttons fit the English labels.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d let them wrap; short labels can triple in length.”

takeaways: Translate whole sentences with named variables and plural cases.
Format numbers, money and dates with locale-aware formatters.
Instants in UTC; future local events as local time plus zone.
Use dir and logical properties for right-to-left layouts.
Plan for short labels to grow two to three times.

interactive.title: How should the booking be stored?
interactive.prompt: A user in London books a video consultation with a doctor in Mumbai for 09:30 Mumbai time, eight months from now. Both should see the right time on the day, even if a time zone’s rules change before then.

choices.label: Local date and time 09:30 plus the zone Asia/Kolkata
choices.feedback: Right: the event is defined by the doctor’s wall clock; each viewer’s local time is computed when it is shown.

choices.label: The UTC instant computed at booking time
choices.feedback: Fine for past events, but a rule change before the date would shift the appointment away from 09:30 in Mumbai.

choices.label: The London time shown to the user when booking
choices.feedback: The doctor’s time is the anchor; London’s offset changes with daylight saving, so this drifts.

interactive.reveal: Instants that already happened go in UTC. Future events anchored to a place keep local time plus that place’s IANA zone, and each viewer’s time is derived at display.

seeAlso.why: Forms that accept names, numbers and dates from any locale
The lang attribute and accessible text that i18n builds on
Font subsets that must cover every script you translate into
Storing and scheduling times on the server: zones, daylight saving and local-time jobs
Unicode normalisation and length limits for translated and user-entered text on the server

title: Real User Monitoring and Front-End Error Tracking
objectives: Collect performance metrics from real visits and report them as percentiles by segment
Send measurements reliably when the page is hidden, at a sampled and affordable volume
Capture, symbolicate and group front-end errors without leaking personal data

cards.title: The lab is one device; users are thousands
cards.body: A lab test runs one page load on one machine and network. Real user monitoring (RUM) measures each real visit in the browser, including load, responsiveness and layout shift, and sends the numbers home. Only field data shows that the checkout is slow on mid-range Android phones in one region while the team’s laptops are fast.

cards.title: Worked example: why the average lies
cards.body: Ten visits have a largest contentful paint of 1.2, 1.3, 1.3, 1.4, 1.5, 1.6, 1.8, 2.1, 4.8 and 9.0 seconds. The mean is 26.0 ÷ 10 = 2.6 s, which describes nobody. The 75th percentile, the value that 75% of visits match or beat, is about 2.1 s, near the 2.5 s “good” threshold, and the slowest 20% wait far longer. Report percentiles, and split them by device, connection and page type.

cards.title: From a visit to a dashboard
cards.body: Measure in the page, send once, aggregate on the server.
steps: Decide once per visit whether it is in the sample
Observe metrics and errors while the page is open
When the page becomes hidden, send one beacon with the final values
Store events with release, page type, device class and connection
Aggregate percentiles and error counts per segment and release

cards.title: Send when the page is hidden, not on unload
cards.body: Some metrics, such as layout shift and interaction latency, are only final when the user leaves. Unload events do not fire reliably on mobile, where users switch apps and the system kills the tab, and unload handlers can stop the page from entering the back-forward cache. Send when the page’s visibility changes to hidden, using the platform beacon call or a request marked keepalive, which survive the page going away.

cards.title: Errors: from “Script error.” to a useful stack
cards.body: A global error handler and an unhandled-rejection handler catch most failures. Errors from scripts on another origin arrive as a bare “Script error.” unless the script is served with CORS headers and loaded with the crossorigin attribute. Production code is minified, so upload source maps for each release to the error service, privately, and symbolicate stacks there. Group by error type and top stack frames, and tag each event with the release so a regression shows up the hour it ships.

cards.title: Trap: collecting personal data by accident
cards.body: URLs carry email addresses and reset tokens in query strings; error messages can include form values. Strip query strings or allowlist parameters, scrub known patterns before sending, never record input contents, and respect consent rules. A monitoring pipeline that leaks personal data turns an observability tool into a privacy incident.

questions.prompt: A dashboard shows mean page load of 2.0 s and the team calls it fine. What should they look at instead?

choices.label: The fastest visit, to see what is possible
The mean again, after removing outliers slower than 5 seconds
The total number of page views per day
The 75th and 95th percentiles split by device class

questions.explanation: Percentiles show what most and the slowest users get, and segments find where it hurts. Trimming outliers hides exactly the users with problems; the fastest visit and raw volume say nothing about experience.

questions.prompt: Interaction latency for long sessions is missing from RUM data on phones. The code sends metrics in an unload handler. What is the fix?

choices.label: Send when the page becomes hidden, using a beacon
Send each metric the moment it is first observed
Ask the user to confirm before leaving the page
Store metrics locally and send them on the next visit only

questions.explanation: Visibility becoming hidden is the last reliable moment on mobile, and beacons survive the page closing. Sending too early misses later updates; a leave prompt harms users; waiting for a next visit loses users who never return.

questions.prompt: Most front-end errors on a site read only “Script error.” with no stack. What is the likely cause?

choices.label: The error service is dropping the stack to save space
The scripts are minified, and minification strips error messages and stack traces
The scripts come from another origin without CORS and the crossorigin attribute
The browser’s console was closed when the errors happened

questions.explanation: Browsers hide details of cross-origin script errors unless the script is loaded in CORS mode. Minified code still has messages and stacks, just with short names that source maps fix.

questions.prompt: A site has 4 million page views a day. Why sample 10% of visits for performance beacons rather than sending all?

choices.label: Browsers refuse to send more than one beacon per minute
400,000 visits a day still give stable percentiles at a tenth of the cost
Sampling drops the slowest visits, which would otherwise distort the percentiles
A sample is needed so that each user is measured only once

questions.explanation: Percentiles from hundreds of thousands of samples are stable; sampling cuts ingest and storage cost. Browsers impose no one-per-minute beacon limit, a sample that dropped slow visits would bias the percentiles rather than fix them, and random per-visit sampling does not guarantee each user is measured only once.

questions.prompt: Order the path of a production error from the browser to a fix.

items.label: The event is grouped with others of the same type and top frames
The event is scrubbed and sent with the release tag
An alert fires when the group spikes after a release
A global handler captures the error and stack
The service symbolicates the stack with that release’s source map

questions.explanation: Capture, clean and tag, make the stack readable, group, then alert on change.

questions.prompt: A site has 3 million page views a day and samples 5% of them for RUM. How many beacons a day does it receive?
assumptions: One beacon per sampled page view
Sampling is random per page view
questions.explanation: Sanity check: still plenty for percentiles, even for a segment with 2% of traffic (3,000 a day).

flashcards.back: RUM measures real visits on real devices; the lab is one controlled run for debugging.
The 75th percentile (and 95th) split by device, connection, page and release.
When visibility becomes hidden, with a beacon; unload is unreliable on mobile.
Cross-origin script without CORS; add the crossorigin attribute and CORS headers.

sources.title: web.dev: Best practices for measuring Web Vitals in the field
Chrome for Developers: Chrome UX Report overview

mechanism.title: How a RUM pipeline works
steps: A small script decides at the start of each visit whether it is in the sample, so a visit is either measured fully or not at all. It then observes navigation timing, largest contentful paint, layout shifts, interactions and long tasks through the browser’s performance observers, and listens for uncaught errors and unhandled promise rejections.

Several values change during the visit: layout shift accumulates, the worst interaction can come late, and a largest paint can be replaced. The script keeps the latest values and sends them when the page’s visibility becomes hidden, the last moment the page is reliably alive on mobile. The platform beacon call queues a small request that completes even if the page is discarded, so one compact payload per visit is enough.

Each event carries the dimensions needed to explain it: page type or route pattern (not the raw URL), release version, device class, effective connection type, country, and whether the load was a first visit or from cache. Raw URLs and free text are scrubbed of personal data before sending.

On the server, metrics are aggregated as percentiles per segment and time window. The 75th percentile matches how Core Web Vitals are assessed, and the 95th shows the tail. Random sampling keeps percentiles unbiased while cutting cost; small segments need longer windows to collect enough samples.

Errors follow a parallel path. The error service receives the minified stack, symbolicates it with the source map uploaded for that release, and groups events by a fingerprint of type, message pattern and top frames. Counts per release reveal regressions, rate limits stop one looping error from flooding storage, and filters drop noise from browser extensions and very old browsers.

useWhen: Any production site where real devices and networks differ from the team’s.
Release processes that need to spot front-end regressions within hours.
avoidWhen: Avoid raw URLs, input contents or personal data in events.
Avoid unload handlers for sending data; they are unreliable and hurt the back-forward cache.

rows: Real devices, networks and user paths
Real users at the 75th percentile, by origin or URL
Your segments, releases and logged-in pages
Costs ingest and needs privacy care

numbers.title: Sizing a sampled RUM pipeline
assumptions: 4 million page views a day
10% random sample per page view
About 1.5 KB per beacon (illustrative)
A segment with 1% of traffic
steps: Ingest: 400,000 × 1.5 KB = 600 MB a day, about 18 GB a month.
Small segment: 400,000 × 0.01 = 4,000 beacons a day, enough for a daily 75th percentile.
At 100% sampling the same pipeline would take 6 GB a day for little extra precision.
numbers.result: A 10% sample keeps percentiles stable for most segments at a tenth of the cost.

india.title: How the public field dataset works
india.label: Official documentation
india.body: Chrome’s documentation describes the Chrome UX Report as a public dataset of real-user experience from opted-in Chrome users, aggregated over a rolling 28-day window and reporting Core Web Vitals at the 75th percentile. web.dev’s field-measurement guidance recommends sending data when the page becomes hidden, avoiding unload handlers, and segmenting by attributes such as device type so that problems for specific users are visible.

pitfalls.trap: “Our average load time is 2 seconds.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d report the 75th and 95th percentiles by device; the mean hides the slow tail.”

pitfalls.trap: “Send the metrics in an unload handler.”
pitfalls.say: “On mobile that often never runs; I’d send when the page becomes hidden.”

pitfalls.trap: “Log the full URL with each error.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d log the route pattern and strip query strings to avoid personal data.”

takeaways: Field data shows what users get; the lab is for debugging.
Report percentiles by segment and release, not means.
Send one beacon when the page becomes hidden.
Upload source maps privately and group errors by fingerprint.
Scrub URLs and messages of personal data.

interactive.title: When should the beacon go?
interactive.prompt: A RUM script must report layout shift and the worst interaction for each visit. Most traffic is mobile, and users often switch apps instead of closing tabs.

choices.label: In an unload handler when the page closes
choices.feedback: Unload often never fires on mobile, and the handler can keep the page out of the back-forward cache.

choices.label: When visibility becomes hidden, with a beacon
choices.feedback: Right: it is the last reliable moment, and a beacon completes even if the page is then discarded.

choices.label: Every second while the page is open
choices.feedback: This multiplies requests and battery use, and still sends values that change later.

interactive.reveal: Keep the latest values in memory and send them when the page becomes hidden; if the user returns and the values change, send an update next time it hides.

seeAlso.why: The metrics and thresholds a RUM pipeline reports
Logging and metrics on the server side that RUM complements
Third-party scripts that often show up in field regressions

title: Focus Management: Dialogs, Menus and Live Regions
objectives: Open and close a modal dialog with correct focus movement, containment and return
Give composite widgets one tab stop with roving focus and arrow keys
Announce changes that do not move focus with live regions, without over-announcing

cards.title: Focus is the keyboard user’s cursor
cards.body: Keyboard and screen reader users act wherever focus is. When content appears, disappears or changes without focus moving with it, they are left typing into nothing, tabbing through hidden content, or unaware anything happened. Focus management means deciding, for every change, where focus goes and what is announced.

cards.title: A modal dialog’s focus lifecycle
cards.body: Move in, stay in, come back.
steps: Remember the element that opened the dialog
Make the rest of the page inert so it cannot be focused or read
Move focus into the dialog: its first field, or its heading if it opens with content
Keep Tab and Shift+Tab inside; Escape closes
On close, return focus to the element that opened it

cards.title: Worked example: deleting the focused row
cards.body: A user tabs to the Delete button on row 7 of 20 and presses Enter. The row is removed, the button with focus is gone, and focus falls back to the document body. A screen reader may announce nothing or lose the user’s place, and where the next Tab lands varies by browser, sometimes the top of the page. Move focus to the same control on the next row, or to the previous row if it was the last, or to the list heading if the list is now empty, and announce “Row deleted”.

cards.title: One tab stop per widget: roving focus
cards.body: A toolbar of 12 buttons should not cost 12 presses of Tab. With roving focus, only the active button is in the tab order; arrow keys move focus within the toolbar, and Tab leaves it. The same pattern serves menus, tabs, radio groups, grids and tree views, as the WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices describe for each widget.

cards.title: Live regions: speak without moving focus
cards.body: Some changes should not steal focus: “3 results found”, “Saved”, a validation summary. Put them in a live region, such as an element with role status, which screen readers announce politely when its text changes. The region must already exist on the page before the text changes; inserting a new region with text in it is often not announced. Use assertive alerts only for urgent problems.

cards.title: Trap: removing the focus outline
cards.body: Designers often remove the browser’s focus outline because mouse users see it after clicks. Keyboard users then cannot tell where they are, which fails the WCAG focus visible criterion. Style focus with the focus-visible pseudo-class, which shows the indicator for keyboard focus but usually not for mouse clicks, and keep it high-contrast and unobscured by sticky headers.

questions.prompt: A modal dialog closes after the user saves. Where should focus go?

choices.label: To the top of the page, so the user can start again
To the element that opened the dialog
To the first link in the main navigation
Nowhere; the browser restores it after the dialog is removed

questions.explanation: Returning focus to the trigger puts the user back where they were. The top of the page or the navigation loses their place, and if the focused element is removed the browser moves focus to the body, not back to the trigger.

questions.prompt: A page has 5 toolbars of 12 buttons each. Which approach gives keyboard users the fewest Tab presses to cross them?

choices.label: Remove the buttons from the tab order and rely on mouse users
Give each button its own tab stop, in visual order
Use roving focus: one tab stop per toolbar, arrows inside
Add a skip link before each button

questions.explanation: Roving focus gives 5 tab stops instead of 60, and arrow keys move within a toolbar. Removing buttons from the tab order makes them unreachable, and skip links per button add stops.

questions.prompt: A search page updates the results count as the user types, but screen readers say nothing. The count is in a new element inserted with its text. What is the fix?

choices.label: Move focus to the count after each keystroke
Use an assertive alert so the count interrupts whatever is being read
Add a tooltip to the search box with the count
Keep a status region on the page and change only its text

questions.explanation: A polite live region present before the change is announced reliably without moving focus. Moving focus interrupts typing, assertive alerts are for urgent messages, and tooltips are not announced on update.

questions.prompt: Which detail makes a modal dialog keyboard-accessible rather than a keyboard trap?

choices.label: Escape and a visible close button both close it and return focus
The dialog covers the full screen on mobile
The dialog has a darker background overlay
Tab moves focus out of the dialog to the page behind it, then back again

questions.explanation: Keeping focus inside a modal is correct as long as the user can leave with standard keys. Size and overlay are visual; letting Tab reach the inert page breaks the modal.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to open and close a modal dialog accessibly.

items.label: Move focus into the dialog
Return focus to the stored element
Store the element that opened the dialog
Keep Tab inside and close on Escape
Make the page behind it inert

questions.explanation: Remember where the user came from, isolate the dialog, move in, contain, then return.

questions.prompt: A page has 5 toolbars with 12 buttons each. With roving focus, how many fewer Tab stops does a keyboard user pass than with one stop per button?
assumptions: Each toolbar becomes one tab stop
No other focusable elements are counted
questions.workedAnswer: 60 stops without roving focus, 5 with it: 60 − 5 = 55 fewer
questions.explanation: Sanity check: crossing the toolbars takes 5 presses instead of 60.

flashcards.back: Store trigger, inert background, focus inside, Tab contained, Escape closes, return focus.
One tab stop per widget; arrow keys move between items.
A live region already on the page, such as role status.
Keep it; style with focus-visible so keyboard users see it.

sources.title: W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: Dialog (Modal) Pattern
W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices: Developing a Keyboard Interface

mechanism.title: How focus moves and how changes are heard
steps: Only one element has focus at a time. Tab and Shift+Tab move through elements in the tab order, which is document order for focusable elements and anything with a tab index of 0; a tab index of −1 makes an element focusable by script but not by Tab. Positive tab index values reorder the page and are best avoided. When the focused element is removed, browsers move focus to the body, so a removal needs a deliberate new target.

A modal dialog takes over interaction. The page behind it is made inert, which removes it from the tab order and from what assistive technology reads, and the dialog is labelled by its heading. Focus moves to the first control, or to the heading if there is text to read first. Tab cycles within the dialog, Escape closes it, and focus returns to the opener. The native modal dialog element provides the inert background, the top layer and Escape handling.

Composite widgets such as toolbars, menus, tabs, listboxes and grids expose one tab stop. With roving focus, the active item has tab index 0 and the others −1; arrow keys move the 0 and the focus, and Home and End jump to the ends. An alternative keeps focus on the container and points at the active item with aria-activedescendant. The Authoring Practices list the expected keys for each widget.

Live regions announce changes that should not move focus. Polite regions, including role status, wait until the screen reader is idle; assertive ones, including role alert, interrupt. The region must exist before its content changes, and messages should be short and not repeated on every keystroke; debounce updates such as result counts.

Focus must be visible and not hidden. WCAG 2.2 requires a visible focus indicator and adds that the focused element must not be entirely hidden by author content such as sticky headers or cookie banners. The focus-visible pseudo-class lets designs show a strong indicator for keyboard users without showing it after every mouse click.

useWhen: Dialogs, drawers, menus, toasts, inline editing and any content that appears or disappears.
Single-page apps where route changes replace content in place.
avoidWhen: Avoid moving focus for passive updates such as counts or autosave; announce them instead.
Avoid positive tab index values to reorder focus; fix the document order.

rows: Its label is read on focus
Yes, to a neighbouring row or the list
Into a dialog if action is needed

numbers.title: Tab stops with and without roving focus
assumptions: 5 toolbars of 12 buttons each
One tab stop per button, or one per toolbar with roving focus
Other focusable elements ignored
steps: Without roving focus: 5 × 12 = 60 tab stops.
With roving focus: 5 tab stops, arrows within each toolbar.
Saved: 60 − 5 = 55 presses to cross the toolbars.
Reaching the 9th button of the 3rd toolbar: 3 Tabs plus up to 8 arrow presses, against 2 × 12 + 9 = 33 Tabs.
numbers.result: Roving focus makes the page as long, in key presses, as its number of widgets rather than its number of controls.

india.title: What the standards ask for
india.label: Official documentation (W3C)
india.body: The W3C WAI-ARIA Authoring Practices Guide documents the modal dialog pattern, including moving focus into the dialog on open, containing Tab, closing on Escape and returning focus to the invoking element, and describes roving tab index and active-descendant techniques for composite widgets. WCAG 2.2 success criteria include Focus Visible, Focus Order, No Keyboard Trap, and the new Focus Not Obscured criteria for sticky content.

pitfalls.trap: “The dialog closes, so we are done.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d return focus to the button that opened it.”

pitfalls.trap: “Remove the outline, it looks ugly after clicks.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d use focus-visible so keyboard users still see it.”

pitfalls.trap: “Move focus to the toast so it gets read.”
pitfalls.say: “A polite live region announces it without stealing focus.”

takeaways: For every change, decide where focus goes and what is announced.
Dialogs: move in, contain, close on Escape, return to the opener.
Composite widgets get one tab stop and arrow keys.
Announce passive updates through an existing live region.
Keep focus visible and unobscured.

interactive.title: Where does focus go?
interactive.prompt: A keyboard user tabs to the Remove button on the third item of a shopping cart and presses Enter. The script deletes the item’s element from the page and updates the total. Nothing else is done about focus.

choices.label: Focus moves to the next item’s Remove button
choices.feedback: Browsers do not pick a neighbour; that is the developer’s job.

choices.label: Focus falls back to the document body
choices.feedback: Right: the focused element is gone, so the body becomes the active element; screen reader users lose their place, and where the next Tab lands varies by browser.

choices.label: Focus stays on the removed button until the next Tab
choices.feedback: A removed element cannot keep focus.

interactive.reveal: Move focus to the next item’s Remove button (or the cart heading if it is empty) and announce “Item removed, total updated” in a polite live region.
