title: A Front-End Testing Strategy
objectives: Choose between unit, component, end-to-end and visual tests by what each can catch and costs
Write tests that find elements the way users do, so refactors do not break them
Quantify and remove flakiness from a test suite

cards.title: Each kind of test answers a different question
cards.body: A unit test asks whether a function computes the right thing: a price formatter, a validation rule. A component or integration test renders part of the interface in a simulated page and checks what a user would see and do. An end-to-end test drives a real browser against a running app and backend. A visual test compares screenshots. Lower layers are fast and precise; higher layers catch wiring, browser and deployment problems.

cards.title: Misconception: more end-to-end tests mean more confidence
cards.body: End-to-end tests are the most realistic, but each takes seconds, touches many services and fails for many unrelated reasons. A suite of hundreds becomes slow and flaky, and teams start ignoring red builds. Cover the critical journeys, such as sign-up, search, checkout, end to end, and push detailed cases such as every validation rule down to component and unit tests.

cards.title: Where to test a checkout form
cards.body: Put each check at the lowest layer that can catch it.
steps: Unit: card number checksum, price and tax rounding
Component: errors show next to the right field and focus moves to the first one
Contract: the client and API agree on the order request shape
End to end: one happy path and one declined card in a real browser
Visual: the form at phone and desktop widths in light and dark themes

cards.title: Find elements like a user does
cards.body: Tests that find a button by a CSS class or a position in the markup break when the markup is refactored, though nothing changed for users. Find elements by role and accessible name (“the button named Pay”), by label for inputs, and by visible text. These tests survive refactors and fail when the interface really changes, and they fail if a control loses its accessible name.

cards.title: Worked example: how flakiness compounds
cards.body: A suite has 500 tests, each failing spuriously one run in a thousand. The chance a run is clean is 0.999 to the power 500, about 0.61, so about 39% of runs fail with no code change. At 1,000 such tests it drops to about 37% clean. A tiny per-test flake rate makes a big suite unreliable, which is why each flaky test must be fixed or quarantined quickly.

cards.title: Trap: waiting with fixed sleeps
cards.body: A test that waits two seconds for a result is slow when the app is fast and flaky when the machine is busy. Wait for a condition instead: the element appears, the request completes, the text changes, with a timeout as a safety net. Also isolate data per test, fake the clock for time-based logic, stub third-party services at the network boundary and disable animations.

questions.prompt: Where should the rule “quantity must be between 1 and 99” be tested most thoroughly?

choices.label: End-to-end tests in a real browser covering each boundary value separately
Unit tests of the validation rule, plus one component test of the message
A visual test of the form with an invalid quantity
Manual testing before each release

questions.explanation: Boundary cases are cheap and precise as unit tests, and one component test proves the message is wired up. End-to-end tests per boundary are slow; screenshots cannot check logic; manual checks do not scale.

questions.prompt: A refactor renames CSS classes, and 40 component tests fail though the page looks and works the same. What change prevents this?

choices.label: Find elements by role, label and accessible name
Snapshot the full markup of each component
Add test-only data attributes to each element
Run the tests only after a manual review

questions.explanation: Role and name queries match how users and assistive technology find controls, so markup changes do not break them. Markup snapshots break on any change; test-only attributes help stability but do not check accessibility; a manual review before running does not stop the queries from breaking.

questions.prompt: An end-to-end test fails about once in 50 runs, only on the CI server, at a step that waits 2 seconds for a list to load. What is the best fix?

choices.label: Raise the wait to 10 seconds
Retry the full suite on the CI server whenever any test fails
Delete the test because it is unreliable
Wait until the list’s items are present, with a timeout

questions.explanation: Waiting for the condition makes the test as fast as the app and tolerant of slow machines. Longer sleeps slow the suite and still fail sometimes, blanket retries hide real bugs, and deleting loses coverage.

questions.prompt: Which problem can only an end-to-end test in a real browser catch?

choices.label: A tax calculation rounding 0.5 the wrong way
An error message rendering under the wrong field after validation
A production build that serves the wrong API base URL
A function returning the wrong date format

questions.explanation: Configuration and wiring across the built app, the network and the backend only show up end to end. Rounding and formatting are unit concerns, and message placement is a component test.

questions.prompt: Order the response to a newly flaky test.

items.label: Find the cause: timing, shared state, order or external calls
Quarantine it so it no longer blocks merges
Fix it and return it to the blocking suite
Reproduce it by running it repeatedly or under load

questions.explanation: Stop the damage, reproduce, find the root cause, then restore the test; quarantine must not become a graveyard.

questions.prompt: A suite has 500 tests and each fails spuriously in 0.1% of runs, independently. About what percentage of runs pass with no spurious failure?
assumptions: Flakes are independent
0.999 to the power 500
questions.workedAnswer: 0.999^500 ≈ e^(−0.5) ≈ 0.61, so about 61% of runs are clean
questions.explanation: Sanity check: the expected number of flakes per run is 500 × 0.001 = 0.5, so a clean run is far from guaranteed.

flashcards.back: The lowest one that can catch the problem; end to end only for critical journeys.
By role, label and accessible name, like users and assistive technology.
500 tests at 0.1% each: about 61% of runs clean.
Wait for a condition with a timeout.

mechanism.title: How the layers fit together
steps: Unit tests run pure logic in milliseconds: formatting, validation, reducers, calculations. They give precise failures and cover edge cases cheaply, but they cannot see rendering, browser behaviour or how pieces are wired together.

Component and integration tests render a piece of the interface in a simulated document or a real browser, interact with it through events, and assert on what appears. Network calls are stubbed at the boundary with realistic responses, ideally generated from the same schema the API uses so the stubs cannot drift. This layer catches most interface bugs at a fraction of end-to-end cost.

Contract tests check that the client and the API agree on requests and responses without running both together. End-to-end tests drive a real browser through the built app against a deployed backend; they catch configuration, routing, authentication and cross-service problems, and they are the slowest and least stable layer, so they cover a few critical journeys.

Visual regression tests take screenshots at fixed viewport sizes and compare them with approved images, catching layout and styling regressions that assertions miss. They need stable fonts, data and animations to avoid noise. Automated accessibility checks run in component or end-to-end tests, but they find only part of the problems, so manual keyboard and screen reader checks are still needed.

Flakiness is non-determinism: timing, shared state between tests, dependence on test order, real time and time zones, randomness and external services. Each source has a fix: wait for conditions, create data per test, fake the clock, seed randomness, stub external calls. Track flaky tests, quarantine them out of the blocking path, and fix them, because the failure probability compounds with suite size.

useWhen: Any front end with more than one developer or frequent releases.
Critical journeys such as sign-up and payment, which need end-to-end coverage.
avoidWhen: Avoid testing every edge case end to end; push it down a layer.
Avoid fixed sleeps and tests that share data or depend on order.

rows: Wiring, configuration, real browser and backend

numbers.title: What flakiness and runtime cost
assumptions: 500 tests, each with a 0.1% spurious failure rate
200 end-to-end tests at 20 s each (illustrative)
8 parallel workers
steps: Clean run probability: 0.999^500 ≈ 0.61, so about 39% of runs fail spuriously.
Halving every flake rate to 0.05%: 0.9995^500 ≈ 0.78 clean.
End-to-end runtime: 200 × 20 s = 4,000 s, about 67 minutes on one worker.
On 8 workers: 4,000 ÷ 8 = 500 s, about 8 minutes if tests are independent.
numbers.result: Small per-test flake rates compound; parallelism only works for isolated tests.

india.title: Flakiness at scale
india.label: Publicly reported (Google Testing Blog, 2016)
india.body: In a 2016 post on the Google Testing Blog, Google reported that about 1.5% of all test runs across its corpus produced a flaky result, meaning the same code both passed and failed, and that almost 16% of its tests showed some level of flakiness. It described mitigations such as re-running failed tests, marking known flaky tests to fail only after three consecutive failures, and tracking flakiness to find causes.

pitfalls.trap: “Let’s cover every validation rule end to end.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d unit-test the rules and keep end to end for the journey.”

pitfalls.trap: “Add a two-second wait so it passes.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d wait for the element or request instead.”

pitfalls.trap: “It’s flaky, just re-run it.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d quarantine and fix it; flakes compound across the suite.”

takeaways: Test each behaviour at the lowest layer that can catch it.
Keep end-to-end tests for a few critical journeys.
Find elements by role and accessible name.
Per-test flakiness compounds: 500 × 0.1% leaves 61% clean runs.
Replace sleeps with conditions; isolate data and clocks.

interactive.title: How often does the suite go red?
interactive.prompt: A team has 500 tests. Each one, independently, fails spuriously in 1 run out of 1,000 even when the code is fine. Predict how often a full run fails with no real bug.

choices.label: About 0.1% of runs, the same as one test
choices.feedback: That is the rate for one test; across 500 tests the chances add up.

choices.label: About 39% of runs
choices.feedback: Right: 0.999 to the power 500 is about 0.61, so 39% of runs have at least one spurious failure.

choices.label: About 5% of runs
choices.feedback: That would need a flake rate of about 0.01% per test, ten times lower.

interactive.reveal: Expected flakes per run are 500 × 0.001 = 0.5, so a clean run is barely more likely than not. Fix or quarantine flaky tests as soon as they appear.

Accessible names that user-style queries rely on
State machines whose transitions are easy to unit-test
Unit, integration and contract tests for the services the UI calls

title: The Cascade, Specificity and Cascade Layers
objectives: Predict which declaration wins using origin, layers, specificity and order
Compute selector specificity, including :is, :not, :where and inline styles
Organise a stylesheet with cascade layers so utilities and overrides win without !important

cards.title: When two rules disagree
cards.body: Most elements match several rules that set the same property. The cascade compares the competing declarations step by step, moving to the next step only on a tie: origin and importance, then cascade layer, then specificity, then order of appearance. So the later declaration wins only when origin, layer and specificity are all equal. Styles set directly in an element’s style attribute sit between importance and layers, beating any selector. Knowing the order turns “why is my style ignored?” into a lookup.

cards.title: The cascade’s tie-breakers in order
cards.body: Each step only matters if all earlier steps tie.
steps: Origin and importance: user-agent, user and author styles; !important reverses their order
Inline style attribute beats any selector in the same origin and importance
Cascade layer: for normal rules, later layers win and unlayered styles beat all layers
Specificity: compare (IDs, classes and attributes and pseudo-classes, types and pseudo-elements)
Order of appearance: the later declaration wins

cards.title: Worked example: comparing specificity
cards.body: Count three columns. nav .menu > li.active a:hover has 0 IDs; .menu, .active and :hover make 3 in the class column; nav, li and a make 3 in the type column: (0, 3, 3). #sidebar a scores (1, 0, 1) and wins, because columns compare left to right and one ID beats any number of classes. Combinators and the universal selector add nothing. :is() and :not() take their most specific argument; :where() always adds zero.

cards.title: Layers: decide the winner by intent, not selector weight
cards.body: Declare the order once: @layer reset, base, components, utilities. A rule in utilities beats a rule in components whatever their specificity, so a one-class utility can override a component styled with an ID. Styles outside any layer beat all layered styles, which lets older or third-party CSS be wrapped in a low layer. For !important declarations the layer order reverses, so an important reset in the first layer beats everything later.

cards.title: Trap: fighting with !important
cards.body: Adding !important to win one battle starts an arms race: the next override needs !important and higher specificity, and so on. Important declarations also reverse the layer order, which surprises people. Fix the structure instead: lower the specificity of component selectors, often with :where(), and put overrides in a later layer.

cards.title: Edge case: inherited values have no weight
cards.body: Properties such as color and font-family inherit from the parent when no rule sets them on the element. An inherited value loses to any rule that targets the element itself, even the browser’s own styles: #article { color: green } does not colour a link inside it, because the user-agent rule for links sets its colour directly. Set the property on the element, or use the inherit keyword in a rule that matches it.

questions.prompt: Which selector has the highest specificity?

choices.label: .card .title .icon .label
main article section p span
#promo a
:where(#promo) .card a

questions.explanation: #promo a is (1, 0, 1). Four classes are (0, 4, 0), five types are (0, 0, 5), and :where() contributes zero, leaving (0, 1, 1). One ID outranks any number of classes.

questions.prompt: Layers are declared as base, components, utilities. A utility rule .mt-0 sets margin-top: 0; a component rule #hero .heading sets margin-top: 2rem. Both are normal declarations. Which applies?

choices.label: margin-top: 2rem, because the component selector is more specific
margin-top: 0, because utilities is a later layer
Whichever rule appears later in the file
Neither; conflicting layers cancel the property

questions.explanation: Layer order is compared before specificity, so the later layer wins for normal declarations. Specificity and source order only break ties within the same layer.

questions.prompt: A third-party widget’s stylesheet is unlayered, and the site’s own styles are all in layers. The widget’s rules keep overriding the site’s. Why?

choices.label: Third-party stylesheets are treated as user-agent styles
The widget’s selectors are more specific than the site’s
Unlayered normal styles beat styles in any layer
Layers apply only to stylesheets on the same origin

questions.explanation: Unlayered author styles form an implicit final layer. Importing the widget’s stylesheet into a low layer with @import and a layer name puts it below the site’s layers.

questions.prompt: An element has style="color: red" and a stylesheet rule #main p { color: blue }. Both are normal declarations. Which colour wins?

choices.label: Blue, because the ID selector is more specific
Blue, if the stylesheet loads after the HTML containing the attribute
Whichever was declared later in the document
Red, because the style attribute beats any selector

questions.explanation: Inline style attributes are ranked above all selectors in the same origin and importance; only !important author rules (or higher origins) beat them.

questions.prompt: Order the cascade’s tie-breakers from first applied to last.

items.label: Specificity
Origin and importance
Order of appearance
Cascade layer
Inline style attribute

questions.explanation: Each later step only decides when everything before it ties.

questions.prompt: How many class-column components (classes, attributes and pseudo-classes) does nav .menu > li.active a:hover[href] have?
assumptions: Types and combinators are not counted in this column
The attribute selector [href] counts as a class-level component
questions.explanation: Sanity check: three type selectors (nav, li, a) go in the third column, which only matters if the first two tie.

flashcards.back: Origin and importance, inline style, layer, specificity, order of appearance.
IDs; classes, attributes and pseudo-classes; types and pseudo-elements.
:where() adds zero; :is() takes its most specific argument.
Beat all layered normal styles; important declarations reverse the layer order.

sources.title: MDN: Introduction to the CSS cascade
W3C: CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 5

mechanism.title: How the browser picks one value
steps: For each element and property, the browser collects every declaration from every stylesheet that matches. If none exists, the value is inherited from the parent for inherited properties, or set to the property’s initial value. If several exist, the cascade sorts them and the winner becomes the cascaded value.

The first criterion is origin and importance. Normal declarations rank user-agent, then user, then author styles, with author winning. Important declarations reverse that: important user-agent beats important user, which beats important author, so users with accessibility style sheets can override sites. Transitions and animations also have their own positions in this ranking.

Within an origin and importance, declarations in an element’s style attribute beat those from selectors. Then come cascade layers. Normal declarations in later-declared layers beat earlier ones, and unlayered declarations beat all layers. Important declarations reverse the order, so important rules in the earliest layer win. Layers can be nested and created by importing a stylesheet into a named layer.

Next is specificity, compared as three numbers: ID selectors; class selectors, attribute selectors and pseudo-classes; type selectors and pseudo-elements. Columns compare left to right without carrying, so (1, 0, 0) beats (0, 15, 0). :is(), :not() and :has() take the specificity of their most specific argument; :where() is always zero, which makes it useful for low-weight base styles that are easy to override.

The final tie-breaker is order of appearance: the declaration that comes later in the combined stylesheets wins. Shorthands set all their longhands, so a later background shorthand resets an earlier background-image. Inheritance is separate from the cascade: an inherited value applies only when no declaration targets the element itself.

useWhen: Design systems where components, themes and utilities must override each other predictably.
Sites mixing their own CSS with third-party or legacy stylesheets.
avoidWhen: Avoid raising specificity or adding !important to win a conflict.
Avoid styling components with ID selectors that are hard to override.

rows: Each override needs even higher specificity
Later layers win regardless of selectors
Unlayered styles still beat all layers

numbers.title: Scoring two selectors
assumptions: Selector A: nav .menu > li.active a:hover
Selector B: #sidebar a
Both in the same layer, both normal declarations
steps: A: IDs 0; classes .menu and .active plus :hover = 3; types nav, li, a = 3: (0, 3, 3).
B: IDs 1; classes 0; types a = 1: (1, 0, 1).
Compare the first column: 1 beats 0, so B wins without looking further.
Wrap A in :where() and it scores (0, 0, 0), so any single class overrides it.
numbers.result: Specificity is compared column by column; one ID outranks any number of classes, and :where() resets weight to zero.

india.title: What the specification defines
india.label: Official specification (W3C)
india.body: The W3C CSS Cascading and Inheritance Level 5 specification defines the cascade sort order as origin and importance, context, element-attached styles, layers, specificity and order of appearance, and introduces the @layer rule. It specifies that unlayered styles are treated as the final layer for normal declarations, and that the order of layers is reversed for important declarations. MDN documents the same order with examples.

pitfalls.trap: “Make the selector more specific to win.”
pitfalls.say: “I’d put the override in a later layer instead of escalating specificity.”

pitfalls.trap: “Add !important, it always wins.”
pitfalls.say: “Important flips the layer order and starts an arms race; I’d fix the structure.”

pitfalls.trap: “The parent is green, so the link should be green.”
pitfalls.say: “Inherited values lose to any rule on the link itself, including the browser’s.”

takeaways: The cascade sorts by origin and importance, inline style, layer, specificity, then order.
Specificity compares IDs, then classes, then types, without carrying.
Later layers win regardless of specificity; unlayered styles win over layers.
Use :where() for low-weight defaults and layers for overrides, not !important.

interactive.title: Which colour does the link get?
interactive.prompt: The site declares @layer base, components. Inside the components layer: #nav a.link { color: red }. Outside any layer, an old stylesheet has a { color: blue }. Both are normal declarations and both match the same link.

choices.label: Red, because its selector is far more specific
choices.feedback: Specificity is compared only within the same layer; the layer decides first.

choices.label: Blue, because unlayered styles beat layered ones
choices.feedback: Right: unlayered normal styles act as a final layer, so a plain type selector beats the layered rule.

choices.label: Whichever stylesheet loads last
choices.feedback: Order of appearance is the last tie-breaker, after layers and specificity.

interactive.reveal: Move legacy and third-party CSS into an early layer, for example by importing it into a legacy layer listed first, so the site’s own layers can override it.

seeAlso.why: The layout properties these cascade rules usually decide
Where style calculation sits in the rendering pipeline
Media queries that add conditional rules to the cascade

title: Third-Party Scripts: Cost and Containment
objectives: Count what a third-party script costs in connections, main-thread time, layout shift and risk
Load third parties late, behind facades, or in sandboxed frames instead of directly in the page
Govern tags with owners, budgets and measurement so the page does not slowly fill up

cards.title: Someone else’s code, with your page’s powers
cards.body: Analytics, ads, chat widgets, video players, A/B testing and tag managers run in your page with the same rights as your own script. They can read the page, every field the user types into, and any cookie not marked HttpOnly, and they can change what the page shows. They also compete for the network and the main thread. Each one is a performance and security decision, usually made by someone outside the front-end team.

cards.title: Worked example: a new origin on the critical path
cards.body: A synchronous script tag in the head loads from a vendor’s origin. Before any byte arrives, the browser needs DNS, TCP and TLS 1.3, about three round trips: at 80 ms each, 240 ms. The request itself adds another round trip, so the first byte arrives after about 320 ms, while the parser waits. If the vendor is slow or down, the page waits until the request times out. Loading it async removes the parser wait; deferring it until after load removes it from the first view.

cards.title: Containment options, weakest to strongest
cards.body: Pick by how much the script needs and how much you trust it.
steps: Load async or after the page is interactive instead of blocking the parser
Show a facade, such as a video thumbnail, and load the real widget on click
Self-host pinned versions with an integrity hash and restrict them with a policy
Run untrusted widgets in a sandboxed iframe on a separate origin
Move analytics collection to your own server endpoint where possible

cards.title: Facades: load the heavy thing on intent
cards.body: A video embed or chat widget can pull hundreds of kilobytes of script on every page view, though most visitors never press play or open the chat. A facade is a lightweight look-alike, such as a thumbnail with a play button or a chat bubble, that loads the real widget when the user interacts. Lighthouse flags embeds that could use facades.

cards.title: Trap: the tag manager as a back door
cards.body: A tag manager lets marketing add scripts without a deploy. That is useful, and it also means code reaches production without review, testing or performance budgets. Give every tag an owner and a purpose, review new tags like code, set a budget for main-thread time and bytes, and remove tags whose campaigns have ended.

cards.title: Edge case: when a vendor is down
cards.body: A vendor outage should cost a feature, not the page. Scripts loaded async or after load fail on their own; a synchronous script in the head or a render-blocking stylesheet from the vendor can blank the page until the browser gives up. Test it by blocking each third-party origin in the browser’s developer tools and checking that the page still renders and works.

questions.prompt: A landing page embeds a video player that downloads about 500 KB of script, and about 5% of visitors press play. What is the best change?

choices.label: Show a thumbnail facade and load the player on click
Preload the player script so it is ready when visitors press play
Move the embed lower on the page
Compress the page’s images more heavily

questions.explanation: A facade spares 95% of visitors the download and main-thread work. Preloading makes it start sooner for everyone, moving it lower may not delay the script, and image compression does not touch the player cost.

questions.prompt: Why can an analytics script read what users type into a payment form on the same page?

choices.label: Browsers grant scripts from trusted vendors extra rights
The vendor’s cookies give it access to the form
Analytics scripts run in a separate process with page access
Every script in the page runs with the page’s own privileges

questions.explanation: Scripts in a page share its origin and access, whatever their source. Cookies and processes are not the reason; there is no trusted-vendor tier. Sensitive fields belong in isolated frames or pages with few scripts.

questions.prompt: The vendor of a synchronous script in the page’s head has an outage, and the page stays blank for about 20 seconds. What prevents this?

choices.label: A preconnect hint so the vendor’s connection opens earlier
Loading the script async or after load, so the parser does not wait
Serving the page’s HTML from a CDN closer to users
A service worker that caches the page’s HTML for repeat visits

questions.explanation: Non-blocking loading makes the vendor’s failure cost only its own feature. Preconnect cannot help when the vendor is down, a closer CDN speeds the HTML but not the vendor’s script, and caching the HTML still leaves the parser waiting on the script.

questions.prompt: Main-thread time from tags grew by 400 ms over a year, one tag at a time. Which practice stops this?

choices.label: Owners, a review for new tags and a main-thread budget
Moving the tag manager to the bottom of the page
Letting each team add tags it needs without review
Asking the vendors to make their scripts faster

mechanism.title: Where third-party cost comes from and how to contain it
steps: Network cost comes first. Each new origin needs DNS, a TCP connection and a TLS handshake before its first request; scripts then often fetch more scripts, pixels and configuration from further origins. A synchronous script blocks the parser until it downloads and runs, so a slow vendor delays the whole page and a down vendor can blank it.

Main-thread cost follows. Third-party code is parsed, compiled and run on the same thread as your own, and it often adds listeners for scroll, clicks and visibility. On mid-range phones this lengthens tasks and raises interaction latency. Ads and embeds inserted without reserved space also cause layout shifts.

Loading strategy is the first lever. Load scripts async, or defer non-essential ones until after the page is interactive or the first user interaction. Use preconnect only for the one or two origins on the critical path. Replace heavy embeds such as video players, maps and chat with facades that load the real thing on intent. Reserve space for ads and embeds so they do not shift content.

Isolation is the second lever. Anything in the page shares its origin and powers. A sandboxed iframe on a separate origin limits what a widget can do: without allow-same-origin it runs in an opaque origin, and capabilities such as scripts, forms and popups must be granted one by one. A Content Security Policy limits where scripts and data can go, and self-hosting a pinned version with an integrity hash stops silent changes.

Governance is the third lever, because third parties accumulate. Keep an inventory of every tag with an owner and purpose, review new tags for privacy, security and performance, set budgets for bytes and main-thread time, and test pages with each vendor blocked. Field monitoring segmented by page shows when a newly added tag causes a regression.

useWhen: Pages with analytics, ads, embeds, chat, A/B testing or tag managers.
Checkout, login and account pages where scripts can read sensitive input.
avoidWhen: Avoid synchronous third-party scripts in the head.
Avoid running untrusted widgets in the main page when a sandboxed frame would do.

india.title: A third-party script host changes owner
india.label: Publicly reported (Sansec, 2024)
india.body: Many sites loaded a browser polyfill directly from the cdn.polyfill.io domain. In February 2024 the domain and its project account were sold to a new owner, and in June 2024 the security firm Sansec reported that the script served from it had been altered to redirect some mobile visitors to scam and betting sites, on more than 100,000 sites that embedded it. The domain’s registrar suspended it days later. Because the file was generated per browser, an integrity hash could not have pinned it; the durable fixes were self-hosting a reviewed copy or removing a polyfill modern browsers no longer needed.

title: UI State Machines: Making Impossible States Impossible
objectives: Spot impossible combinations created by independent boolean flags
Model a component as explicit states, events and transitions
Use the model to ignore invalid events, such as a second submit, and to drive tests

cards.title: Boolean soup
cards.body: A data panel tracks isLoading, isError and hasData as three separate flags. Three booleans allow 2³ = 8 combinations, but only four are meaningful: idle, loading, success and error. The other four, such as loading and error at once, are bugs waiting to happen: a spinner over an error message, or stale data shown as fresh. Each new flag doubles the combinations again.

cards.title: Misconception: a state machine needs a library
cards.body: A state machine is just three things: a single variable holding the current state, a list of events, and a table saying which event moves which state where. A switch over the state, or a lookup table, is enough. Libraries add visual tools and nested states, but the idea is a design discipline, not a dependency.

cards.title: A payment button as a state machine
cards.body: Each state lists the events it accepts; others are ignored.
steps: idle: on submit, go to submitting and send the request
submitting: on success go to paid; on failure go to failed; ignore submit
failed: on retry go to submitting; show the error
paid: terminal; ignore submit and retry
Data lives with its state: the error message only in failed, the receipt only in paid

cards.title: Worked example: the double charge
cards.body: If the only guard is a disabled button that appears on the next render, a fast double click can fire two submit handlers first, sending two payment requests. In a state machine, every click is sent to the machine as an event, the first one moves idle to submitting as it is processed, before any render, and submitting has no transition for submit, so the second click does nothing. Pair it with an idempotency key so even a retry after a timeout cannot charge twice.

cards.title: Trap: keeping data in states where it is meaningless
cards.body: If the error message is a separate field, it survives into the next success and is shown with fresh data. Attach data to the state that owns it: the error only exists in failed, the results only in success, and the previous results in a refreshing state if you want to keep showing them while reloading. Then showing stale data becomes a choice you write down, not an accident.

cards.title: Edge case: states that run in parallel
cards.body: A video player is playing or paused, and independently muted or unmuted, and fullscreen or not. Modelling every combination as one flat list gives 2³ = 8 states that are hard to maintain. Statecharts, introduced by David Harel in the 1980s, allow parallel regions and nested states, so each concern stays a small machine of its own.

mechanism.title: How explicit states remove a class of bugs
steps: Interface code often grows one flag at a time: a loading flag, then an error flag, then a refreshing flag. Each handler flips the flags it knows about. With n flags the code can represent 2 to the power n combinations, and nothing stops it reaching the invalid ones. Bugs appear as screens that show two things at once or carry leftovers from an earlier state.

A finite state machine replaces the flags with one value naming the current state, such as idle, loading, success or failure. Events, such as a user submit or a server response, are sent to the machine. A transition table says, for each state, which events it accepts and which state comes next; an event with no entry for the current state is ignored. Rendering is a function of the current state.

Data travels with states. In a typed language this is a tagged union: the success variant carries results, the failure variant carries an error, and the loading variant may carry the previous results if the design keeps them visible. Code cannot read results in the failure state because they do not exist there. Side effects, such as sending a request or moving focus, are attached to transitions, so they run exactly when the state changes.

Because the machine ignores events it does not expect, races become explicit decisions. A second submit while submitting is ignored. A response that arrives after the user cancelled finds the machine in idle, where it has no transition, so it is dropped. For overlapping requests, the state can hold the id of the request it is waiting for and accept only that response.

Bigger interfaces need structure. Statecharts, introduced by David Harel and standardised in notation such as the W3C’s SCXML, add nested states that share transitions, parallel regions for independent concerns, and guards on transitions. The model doubles as documentation and a test plan: one test per transition and one per ignored event covers the component’s behaviour.

useWhen: Components with asynchronous work: forms, uploads, payments, wizards, media players.
Flows where a double action or a late response would cause real damage.
avoidWhen: Avoid for simple toggles where one boolean is the whole state.
Avoid one flat machine for independent concerns; use parallel regions.

numbers.result: A single state variable shrinks 16 representable combinations to the 5 that are real.

india.title: The notation behind statecharts
india.label: Official specification (W3C) and public history
india.body: The W3C’s State Chart XML recommendation defines a standard notation for state machines with nested and parallel states, events, guards and actions, based on Harel statecharts. In his paper for the ACM History of Programming Languages conference in 2007, David Harel describes how statecharts grew out of specifying the behaviour of complex reactive avionics systems, where flat state diagrams became unmanageable.
